Low sun turns the flying white water to molten gold while the wet black rock behind it stays black as coal, the two colours refusing to meet.
A black storm wall stands far out over the water; the pink flowers on the near slope blaze electric in front of it, lit as if from inside.
Hard noon sun drives razor shadows into every crack in the stone; the water below has gone deep ink-blue, almost purple at the edges.
One break in the cloud drops a single bright patch onto one bank of flowers, turning them fierce magenta while the whole surrounding slope goes slate-grey.
Backlight coming low through the petals so they read as lit coloured glass, amber and rose, with the wet rock behind them almost black.
The last gold light has left the flowers and is climbing the rock behind them, a warm amber line rising against the grey while the blooms drop into blue shadow.
Sun after a shower with every surface mirror-bright; the orange lichen on the rock is burning, almost too orange to be real against the cold blue sky.
A rainbow stands against the retreating rain out over the water, one foot violet, one foot red, the grey sea beneath it gone briefly luminous.
Grey sea fog pours in over the edge and erases the far water entirely; only the near flowers remain in colour, vivid pink against absolute white.
Cold blue dusk and the white foam below is still bright, the last light of the day somehow caught in that flying white water while everything above it turns indigo.
A hail shower has left small white stones bright among the pink flowers, each stone catching light so the slope glitters between the colour.
Moonlight silvers the wet rock so it reads white, while the water below runs entirely in black and white, all colour evacuated from the frame.
The sky shades from pale cold lemon at the horizon to deep near-violet at the top of the frame; the flowers below catch the lemon and go a warm impossible gold.
Sun so low it comes in almost level and lights only the undersides of the leaves, turning them lime-gold while their tops stay deep shadow-green.
The thin dark soil between the flowers is catching the orange last light and reading as red-brown, a warm streak running right across the cold grey of the bare rock.
Cloud shadow sweeps the slope and for one second only the flowers at the very edge are lit, a hard-lit strip of pink against the dark blue open water below.
Flat bright overcast presses everything down; then the sun punches one clean hole and a column of gold hits the wet stone, turning the orange lichen incandescent.
A squall has left the air rinsed and the near flowers are vivid pink-magenta against a sky that has gone an almost violent clean blue behind the last dark cloud.
The light is failing fast and the foam below is the brightest thing in the frame, white and restless against the water that has turned near-black.
Double light: pink from the sky behind the camera and gold from the low sun still touching the flowers, the two colours meeting on the petals and doing something unlikely.
Salt mist catches the slant sun so the air itself above the flowers glows faint gold, the blooms beneath it going darker by contrast, almost red.
Early morning, the sun not yet above the horizon; the sky is a cold pale gold strip and the flowers on the top of the slope are catching it, the rock below them still in blue-grey dark.
The cloud breaks late and rakes long warm shadows from every tuft of wiry grass across the pale rock, the shadow-lines going amber-grey across near-white stone.
A thin veil of rain moves right across the slope; behind it the flowers read as smeared magenta, but in front of it where the sun still hits they are clean and hard and crimson.
Deep winter light so low and so amber it turns the scoured wiry grass from yellow-green to raw gold while the water behind it stays a cold flat grey-green, the two refusing to agree.
